passage:
Monday. The module guide said AI tools could be used only for spelling and grammar, with a note declaring it. At midnight Aadhya stared at her half-finished analysis, and the urge to paste the whole assignment into a chatbot felt loud.
Wednesday. She didn't. She wrote the analysis herself, badly at first, and asked her labmate Ira to test her by asking why each step was there. She stumbled twice and went back to the data.
The next Monday. Aadhya submitted with a short line: "Grammar check by an AI tool." In the follow-up discussion the tutor asked her to justify one method. Aadhya answered without notes. Outside, Ira asked how it went. "I actually know it," Aadhya said, grinning.

qa.q: What did the module guide allow AI tools to be used for?
qa.a: It allowed them only for spelling and grammar, with a note declaring it.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling at midnight on Monday?
qa.a: She was tempted and under pressure, and the urge to paste the whole assignment felt loud.

qa.q: Why was writing the analysis herself the wiser choice?
qa.a: She could explain and defend it, so she really had the competence. Being caught costs less than lacking skill she claimed.

qa.q: How might the tutor have seen Aadhya's declared line and her answer?
qa.a: The tutor likely saw someone following the rule, and the question about one method tested whether she understood what she submitted.

grounding: Temptation to pass AI work off as her own where it is not allowed: she follows the rules, discloses, and understands what she submits.
